title: Creating Adaptive Space
author: Nick Hart
summary: Working from Uhl-Bien and Arena on organisational adaptability and Schulze and Pinkow on adaptive space, Hart argues that adaptability is a property of the organisation rather than a trait of its leader. Adaptive space is defined as the arena where an organisation's entrepreneurial and operational systems meet, the place where new ideas are tested, connected and eventually absorbed into the operational core. Applied to schools, this reframes improvement: schools evolve not when a leader writes a strategy but when professional knowledge about assessment, curriculum or pedagogy is reconfigured through interaction until it works in context. Hart develops the paired dynamics of conflicting and connecting, warning that over-managing conflict dissipates its energy while ignoring it fragments innovation. A worked example about redesigning an assessment system shows leaders declining to settle a disagreement and instead introducing decision-making boundaries such as threshold concepts, recurrence, weighting and criticality, which converts the task into a leadership development opportunity. Networks are presented as the circulatory system of adaptability, carrying ideas between people who see the school from different angles. The final section turns to design: time protected as a leadership resource, physical and virtual spaces that let ideas cross boundaries, and meetings treated as adaptive infrastructure rather than compliance exercises.
points: The assessment example is the piece's most transferable idea: giving a stuck team decision-making criteria rather than a decision turns a task into professional learning.
Hart's reading of Lencioni positions conflict around ideas as a productive team behaviour, and warns that unchallenged claims from high-status people quietly stunt a school's adaptability.
Treating time as a leadership resource has concrete implications, including protecting thinking time during improvement phases and stripping administratively heavy meetings.
Because innovation travels through informal relationships long before it reaches documents, Hart argues leaders should attend to the pattern of interaction rather than the structure on paper.
The design question he poses for every meeting, whether the space helps people explore and connect or merely comply, is a usable audit of a school's meeting calendar.
quotes: Adaptability is a capability of the organisation itself, the way it continually transforms its own knowledge, routines and relationships in response to context. For schools, that means adaptability is a property of how the community thinks and works together.

Schools don’t evolve because a leader writes a new strategy. They evolve when professional knowledge is continually reconfigured through interaction, when ideas about assessment, curriculum, or pedagogy are shared, tested, and adapted until they work in context.
Conflicting creates the energy for change; friction between the new and the established. Connecting allows those ideas to flow across boundaries and into the formal system. Both are necessary.

When leaders over-manage conflict, the energy dissipates; when they ignore it, innovation fragments. Adaptive leadership is the discipline of holding the tension long enough for something better to form.
Innovation travels through informal relationships long before it appears in documents. Leaders who understand this pay as much attention to the pattern of interaction as to the structure on paper.
Every example of adaptive space began with time to think. For school leaders, this finding reframes how we treat time: it’s a leadership resource.
Leaders can treat every meeting as a design choice: is this space helping people to explore and connect, or merely to comply?
